newsitem.title: FRANCE: French truckers dig in at icy barricades.
newsitem.headline: French truckers dig in at icy barricades.

text.p: Huddled around a fire with hot coffee and biscuits in the middle of the barricaded A1 motorway to Belgium, French truck drivers vowed to maintain their blockade despite a government appeal to return to work.

In freezing temperatures before dawn on Thursday, drivers who have been blocking highways, borders and fuel depots for the last 11 days listened sceptically to radio reports of the breakdown of talks with employers and the government.

"They are offering us a one percent pay rise, it's ridiculous. We are demanding 10 percent. A fair deal would be around five percent," said Dany, a delivery man who normally transports fresh produce to local hypermarkets.
"Our wages are a joke," said Dany, a married man in his 40s. "Since the last big strike in 1992, I've lost 4,000 francs ($800) a month net because of recent tax changes."

Watched from a distance by a handful of police, the strikers debated the outcome of the talks, weighing the achievement of retirement at 55 instead of 60 for drivers with 25 years at the wheel against the absence of progress on pay.

"I expect more from this action," said Gerard, father of a young girl, his eyes red with exhaustion. "We won't be fooled like we were in 1992, when we lifted the barricades only to realise afterwards that the bosses didn't keep their promises.
"We have to do everything ourselves nowadays. We have to fill in the paperwork, load and unload as well as drive. We've become transport technicians' for a pauper's wages," he said.
Pierre, a 23-year-old heavy goods vehicle driver from Clermont-Ferrand in central France, said pay was the key issue for him.
"Earning 7,000 francs ($1,400) for a 200-hour month at the wheel of a 44-tonne truck isn't much," he said. The drivers are demanding a 10,000 franc ($2,000) wage for a 200-hour month.
The truckers keep in touch with comrades manning barricades around the country, and with their union headquarters in Paris, by cellphone.
For lunch, they cook up steaks taken from a refrigerated transport truck, but well past their sell-by date.
In the evenings, the local motorway truck-stop restaurant has cooked them a hot evening meal for a give-away price.
In other gestures of public support, local residents have brought them firewood or taken strikers home for a shower.
Asked how long they could go on, Pierre said: "Nothing will stop us. I'm not married, so I don't have a wife to go home to on Friday night."

Just across the border in Belgium, French motorists queue for petrol at filling stations. Most petrol stations on the French side of the border have run out or been requisitioned to provide fuel only for priority public service vehicles.
Cross-border commuters use back roads to get to their jobs on both sides of the frontier while the motorway is blocked.
